3431.title: One Chance
english_paragraphs: A man wanted to learn archery, so he found a skilled archer to teach him. He picked up a bow and two arrows, ready to take a practice shot. Just then, his teacher came over, took one of the arrows, and threw it on the ground.
“Why did you take away my second arrow?” the student asked in surprise.
“I didn’t take away your second arrow. I took away your first. You wouldn’t have hit the target with it anyway,” the teacher explained.
“Why not?” the student asked, puzzled.
“If you keep thinking you have another chance when you shoot, you won’t make the most of your first chance. So it makes no difference whether you have that first arrow,” the teacher replied.
3431.english_full:
A man wanted to learn archery, so he found a skilled archer to teach him. He picked up a bow and two arrows, ready to take a practice shot. Just then, his teacher came over, took one of the arrows, and threw it on the ground.

“Why did you take away my second arrow?” the student asked in surprise.

“I didn’t take away your second arrow. I took away your first. You wouldn’t have hit the target with it anyway,” the teacher explained.

“Why not?” the student asked, puzzled.

“If you keep thinking you have another chance when you shoot, you won’t make the most of your first chance. So it makes no difference whether you have that first arrow,” the teacher replied.
russian_paragraphs: Мужча́рина жела́л учи́ться стрельбе́ из лу́ка, поэ́тому он осно́вал иску́сного лу́чника, чтобы на́учить его́. Он взя́л лу́к и две стрелы́, гото́вый к пра́ктическому вы́стрелу. Тогда́ его́ наста́вник подошёл, взял одну́ из стрел и бро́сил её́ на землю́.
«Почему́ ты забра́л мою втору́ю стрелу́?» — спра́шивает сту́дент, озада́ченный.
«Я не забрал твою втору́ю стрелу́. Я забрал твою пе́рвую. С ней ты всегдá не попа́дёшь в мише́нь», — объясни́л наста́вник.
«Почему́ бы и нет?» — спра́шивает сту́дент, озада́ченный.

«Если ты продо́лжишь дужи́ть, что у тебя ес́ть друго́й шанс, когда ты стреля́ешь, ты не использо́вaшь по́лностью свой пе́рвый шанс. Поэтому́ не́т ни́кaкой ра́зницы, есть у тебя эта́ пе́рвая стрела́ или нет», — ответил наста́вник.
reading_paragraphs: Mužčína želáł učít'sja streľbé iz lúka, poétomu on osnóval iskúsného lúčnika, čtoby naúčit' egó. On vzjá́l lúk i dve strelý, gotovýj k práktičeskomu výstrelu. Tadá egó naštávnik podošёл, vzjâl odnú iz strél i brósil éj na zemľú.
«Pčómu ty zabrál moju vtorúju strélu?» — sprášíva stúdónt, ozadáčennyj.
«Ja ne zabral tvoju vtorúju strélu. Ja zabral tvoju pérvuju. S néj ty vségda ne popadëš' v mišeń», — ob'jasníl naštávnik.
«Pčómu by i net?» — sprášíva stúdónt, ozadáčennyj.

«Eslí ty prodoĺžиш' dúžit', čto u tebja eśt' drúgoj šans, kadá ty streľáješ', ty ne ispol'zováješ' pólnost'ju svoj pérvyj šans. Poétomu nét níkakoj ráznicy, eśt' u tebja etá pérvaja stréla ili net», — otvetil naštávnik.

3892.title: The Essence of Learning
english_paragraphs: Once, a student asked his teacher, “Teacher, could you tell me the essence of all your wisdom? Then I could become as wise as you.”

The teacher smiled, picked up an apple, and took a big bite. He looked at his student as he chewed it. After a while, he spat the chewed-up apple into his hand and held it out to the student. “Eat this!” he said. The student exclaimed in surprise, “Teacher! How... how could I eat that?” The teacher replied, “You know you can’t eat an apple I’ve already chewed. The essence of my wisdom is like this chewed-up apple. I could give it to you directly, but it would have lost its original fresh, sweet taste. To learn, you need to chew things over and experience them for yourself. Many answers can only be found through your own thinking.”

Once, a student asked his teacher, “Teacher, could you tell me the essence of all your wisdom? Then I could become as wise as you.”

The teacher smiled, picked up an apple, and took a big bite. He looked at his student as he chewed it. After a while, he spat the chewed-up apple into his hand and held it out to the student. “Eat this!” he said. The student exclaimed in surprise, “Teacher! How... how could I eat that?” The teacher replied, “You know you can’t eat an apple I’ve already chewed. The essence of my wisdom is like this chewed-up apple. I could give it to you directly, but it would have lost its original fresh, sweet taste. To learn, you need to chew things over and experience them for yourself. Many answers can only be found through your own thinking.”
russian_paragraphs: Одна́жды студе́нт спра́шивал своего́ наста́вника: "Наста́вник, ты не мог бы ска́зать мне су́щность всей твоей му́дрости? Тогдá я мог бы стать та́ким же му́дрым, как ты."

Наста́вник улыбну́лся, взя́л я́блоко и отку́сил от него́ большо́й кусо́к. Он смо́трел на своего́ студе́нта, пока он жевал я́блоко. По́сле неко́торого вре́мени он сплю́нул жева́нное я́блоко к себе́ в ру́ку и протя́нул его́ студе́нту. "Съешь э́то!" — ска́зал он. Студе́нт воскли́кнул с сюрпри́зом: "Наста́вник! Как... как я могу́ съесть э́то?" Наста́вник ответи́л: "Ты зна́ешь, ты не смо́жешь съесть я́блоко, кото́рое я уже́ жевал. Су́щность моей́ му́дрости похо́жа на э́то жева́нное я́блоко. Я мог бы дать её тебе́ напря́му, но оно́ бы потеря́ло свой первонача́льный све́жий, сла́дкий вкус. Чтоб учи́ться, нужно жева́ть вещи́ и пережива́ть их самостоя́тельно. Мно́гие отве́ты могут бы́ть найдены только через твоё собственное мы́шление."

3633.title: We Are Rich
english_paragraphs: Once there was a young man who complained every day that he had no money. One day, an old man passing by saw how dejected he was and asked, “Why are you so down?” The young man replied, “I have no money, and my life is terrible. It makes me miserable.” The old man said, “That’s easy! I’ll give you ten thousand yuan for your hands. Then you’ll have money.” The young man said angrily, “What kind of solution is that? I wouldn’t sell them for a million yuan, let alone ten thousand!” The old man smiled and said, “See? Aren’t you rich already? Why can’t you use your hands to earn money, just as other people do?” Suddenly, the young man understood. He thanked the old man, found a job, and eventually changed his life.
No matter what difficulties we face, things can turn out differently if we think about them and face them with a positive attitude.
3633.english_full:
Once there was a young man who complained every day that he had no money. One day, an old man passing by saw how dejected he was and asked, “Why are you so down?” The young man replied, “I have no money, and my life is terrible. It makes me miserable.” The old man said, “That’s easy! I’ll give you ten thousand yuan for your hands. Then you’ll have money.” The young man said angrily, “What kind of solution is that? I wouldn’t sell them for a million yuan, let alone ten thousand!” The old man smiled and said, “See? Aren’t you rich already? Why can’t you use your hands to earn money, just as other people do?” Suddenly, the young man understood. He thanked the old man, found a job, and eventually changed his life.

No matter what difficulties we face, things can turn out differently if we think about them and face them with a positive attitude.
russian_paragraphs: Одна́жды был молодо́й челове́к, кото́рый кажды́й день жа́лова́лся, что у него́ нет ба́бок. Одна́жды, прохожи́й де́душка уви́дел, нака́кое он мра́чный и спра́шивает: «Почему́ ты так пода́влен?» Молодо́й челове́к о́тветил: «У меня́ нет ба́бок, и моя́ жизнь ужа́сна. Это дела́ет меня́ несча́стным.» Де́душка ска́зал: «Это про́сто! Я дам тебе де́сять ты́сяч юа́нь за твои́ руки. Тогда́ у тебя́ будут ба́бки.» Молодо́й челове́к гне́вно ска́зaл: «Како́е это реше́ние? Я не стал бы продава́ть их ни за миллио́н юа́нь, не говоря́ уже о де́сяти ты́сячах!» Де́душка усмеха́лся и ска́зал: «Ви́дишь? Разве ты́ не бога́т уже́? Почему́ ты не мо́жешь испо́льзовать свои́ руки́, чтобы зарабатывать деньги́, как и друго́и́ лю́ди?» Вдруг моло́дой челове́к поня́л. Он поблагодари́л де́душку, нашёл рабо́ту и в ито́ге изменил свою́ жизнь.
Несмо́тря на то́, с какими сло́жностями мы сталкива́емся, ве́щи могут ока́зываться по-друго́му, если мы обду́маем их и встре́тим с позити́вным у́глом.
reading_paragraphs: Odnázhdy byl molodói chelovék, kotoryi kázdyi denʹ zhalovalsya, chto u nego net bábok. Odnázhdy, prokhozhii dédushka uvidél, nakákoe on mrácnyy i spráshivaet: «Pochému ty tak podávlen?» Molodói chelovék otvétíl: «U menya net bábok, i moya zhiznʹ uzhásna. Éto deláyet menya neschástnym.» Dédushka skázal: «Éto prósto! Ya dam tebe désyatʹ tysích yuán za tvoyí ruki. Togdá u teba budut bábki.» Molodói chelovék gnévno skázal: «Kakóe éto reshéniye? Ya ne stal by prodavátʹ ikh ni za millíon yuán, ne govoryá uzhe o désyati tysích!» Dédushka usmekhalsya i skázal: «Vidísh? Razve ty ne bogát uzhe? 3222.title: Fairness
english_paragraphs: Two little dogs were fighting fiercely over a cookie. Just then, a big dog came over. The little dogs saw a way to settle their argument. They stopped fighting and asked the big dog to divide the cookie for them.

The big dog broke the cookie in half, and each little dog got a piece. But one little dog told the big dog that its piece was smaller, so the big dog took a bite out of the other dog’s piece. Then the other little dog said its piece was now smaller, so the big dog took a bite out of the first dog’s piece. The little dogs kept arguing, and the big dog kept taking bites. In the end, the big dog ate the whole cookie.
It turns out that fairness is just about making both sides feel things are even!
3222.english_full:
Two little dogs were fighting fiercely over a cookie. Just then, a big dog came over. The little dogs saw a way to settle their argument. They stopped fighting and asked the big dog to divide the cookie for them.

The big dog broke the cookie in half, and each little dog got a piece. But one little dog told the big dog that its piece was smaller, so the big dog took a bite out of the other dog’s piece. Then the other little dog said its piece was now smaller, so the big dog took a bite out of the first dog’s piece. The little dogs kept arguing, and the big dog kept taking bites. In the end, the big dog ate the whole cookie.

It turns out that fairness is just about making both sides feel things are even!
russian_paragraphs: Два́ ма́леньких пса́ бью́щими́сь жесто́ко спорили́ из-за пече́нья. То́гда́ большо́й пёс пришёл. Ма́ленькие псы́ уви́дели́ спосо́б у́ладить свой спор. Они́ прекрати́ли ссо́ру и спра́шивали большо́го пса́, чтобы он раздели́л пече́нье для них.

Большо́й пёс разде́лил пече́нье пополам, и ка́ждый ма́ленький пёс получи́л кусо́к. Но один ма́ленький пёс ска́зал большо́му псу́, что его́ кусо́к меньший, и большо́й пёс отку́сил у друго́го пса́ кусо́к. То́гда друго́й ма́ленький пёс ска́зал, что его́ кусо́к те́перь меньший, и большо́й пёс отку́сил у пе́рвого пса́ кусо́к. Ма́ленькие псы́ продолжа́ли спо́рить, а большо́й пёс продолжа́л отку́сывать. В конце́ концо́в большо́й пёс съел целое пече́нье.
Ока́зывается, что справедли́вость — это просто о том, чтобы обе стороны́ чувствовали, что всё ро́вно!

3325.title: Sowing and Harvesting
english_paragraphs: A man passing through an oasis saw an old man planting seeds. He walked over and asked, “Hello, sir. What are you doing out here in this heat?”
“I’m planting date palms,” the old man replied.
“Date palms?” the man asked. “Sir, how old are you?”
“I don’t know—sixty, seventy, or maybe eighty. I’ve forgotten. But it doesn’t matter.”
The young man said, “Sir, a date palm takes more than fifty years to grow, and it can only bear fruit after that. You probably won’t live to harvest any dates, so why not stop?”
But the old man said, “The dates I eat come from trees planted by those who came before me. I’m planting these trees today so those who come after me can eat their dates.”

«Я сажаю фи́никовые па́льмы,» отвеча́ет дя́дя.
«Фи́никовые па́льмы?» спра́шивает мужчина. «Господи́н, сколько вам тво́л?»

3246.title: Stick to Your Choice
english_paragraphs: Once, three brothers left the countryside for the city, hoping to build businesses of their own. After overcoming many difficulties, they finally reached a bustling town. Three roads led out of the town. People said only one reached the city, but no one knew which one it was. Each brother chose a different road. Thirty years later, the two older brothers were still living in poor mountain villages, while the youngest had a company of his own. As it turned out, all three roads were difficult, full of challenges and hardship. The older brothers doubted their choices, so they gave up when they ran into trouble. But the youngest never forgot an elder’s advice: “Follow the path you believe is right.” He trusted his choice and kept going to the end.
In fact, every road could lead to the city. Follow the path you believe is right, and keep going. You are sure to succeed.

Once, three brothers left the countryside for the city, hoping to build businesses of their own. After overcoming many difficulties, they finally reached a bustling town. Three roads led out of the town. People said only one reached the city, but no one knew which one it was. Each brother chose a different road. Thirty years later, the two older brothers were still living in poor mountain villages, while the youngest had a company of his own. As it turned out, all three roads were difficult, full of challenges and hardship. The older brothers doubted their choices, so they gave up when they ran into trouble. But the youngest never forgot an elder’s advice: “Follow the path you believe is right.” He trusted his choice and kept going to the end.

In fact, every road could lead to the city. Follow the path you believe is right, and keep going. You are sure to succeed.
russian_paragraphs: Одина́жды три бра́та у́шли из се́льской ме́стности в го́род, наде́ясь постро́ить свои́ бизнéсы. После преодоле́ния мно́гих сло́жностей они́ наконе́ц до́шли до переполоха́ и суеты́ города. Три доро́ги вели́ из города. Лю́ди ска́зали, что только одна дорога доходит до го́рода, но никто́ не знал, какой из них. Каждый брат выбрал другую доро́гу. Тридцать лет по́зже два ста́рших брата всё ещё жи́ли в бедных го́рах, в то вре́мя как са́мый мла́дший имел свою́ компа́нию. Как ока́залось, все три доро́ги были́ тру́дными, полными вызовов и невзгод. Ста́ршие братья сомнева́лись в своём вы́боре, поэтому они́ сдались, когда столкну́лись с затрудне́нием. Но мла́дший никогда́ не забы́вал сове́т ста́ршего: «Следуй по той тропе́, в ко́торую ты веришь». Он довере́л своему́ вы́бору и шёл до конца́.
В действи́тельности каждая дорога могла́ привести́ в го́род. Следуй по той тропе́, в ко́торую ты веришь, и продолжай идти́. Ты обя́зательно преуспе́ешь.

3203.title: Know and Achieve
english_paragraphs: Once, Jack Welch, the CEO of General Electric, was invited to China to speak to business managers. But after his talk, many of them felt disappointed. They asked him, “We already know most of what you told us, so why is the gap between us so large?” Welch replied, “Because you only know what to do, while I have actually done it. That’s the difference between us.”

To go from knowing to doing, you have to take action and overcome all kinds of difficulties. There are roughly two reasons why many people know what to do but fail to do it: some lack the willingness to work hard and cannot see things through to the end; others stop at talking about what they know and never act.
If you never try and never keep at it, then even if you know what to do, success will remain nothing more than talk.
3203.english_full:
Once, Jack Welch, the CEO of General Electric, was invited to China to speak to business managers. But after his talk, many of them felt disappointed. They asked him, “We already know most of what you told us, so why is the gap between us so large?” Welch replied, “Because you only know what to do, while I have actually done it. That’s the difference between us.”

To go from knowing to doing, you have to take action and overcome all kinds of difficulties. There are roughly two reasons why many people know what to do but fail to do it: some lack the willingness to work hard and cannot see things through to the end; others stop at talking about what they know and never act.

If you never try and never keep at it, then even if you know what to do, success will remain nothing more than talk.
russian_paragraphs: О́дин раз Джек Уэлч, генди́р компа́нии «Дже́нера́л Электрик», был приглаше́н в Кита́й, чтобы поговори́ть с ме́неджерами би́знеса. Но по́сле его́ бе́седы мно́гие из них остались разочаро́ванными. Они́ спра́шивали его́: «Мы уже́ зна́ем большинствó из того́, что вы́ сказа́ли нам, так почему́ же интерва́л ме́жду на́ми так кру́пный?» Уэлч отве́тил: «Потому что вы́ только зна́ете, что де́лать, в то вре́мя как я факти́чески согласи́лся это сде́лать. Вот ра́зница ме́жду на́ми.»

Чтобы перейти́ от зна́ния к де́йствию, вы́ до́лжны при́нять а́кции и преодолева́ть все ро́ды тру́дностей. Прибли́зительно две причи́ны, по ко́торым мно́гие лю́ди зна́ют, что де́лать, но не удаю́тся сде́лать это: некоторые́ не́ хватает жела́ния рабо́тать усердно и не мо́гут довести́ де́ло до ко́нца; дру́гие остаются на уровне разго́вора о том, что они́ зна́ют, и никогда́ не де́йствуют.
Если вы́ никогда́ не пробу́ете и никогда́ не будете продолжа́ть это, то да́же е́сли вы́ зна́ете, что де́лать, успе́х оста́нется ничем бо́льше, чем разго́вор.
reading_paragraphs: Ódin raz Dzhek Uélch, gendír kompánii «Dzhenerál Élektrik», byl prigláshen v Kitáy, chtoby pogovorít' s méndzherami bíznesa. No pósle egó besédy mnógie iz nikh ostalis' razocharovánnymi. Oný spráshivali egó: «My užé známe bol'shinstvó iz tógo, chto vy skazáli nam, tak pochemú zhe intervál mézhdu námi tak krúpny?» Uélch otvétil: «Potomu chto vy tól'ko znáte, chto delát', v to vremya kak ya faktícheski soglasílsya éto sdelát'. Vót ráznica mézhdu námi.»

Chtoby peredít' ot znánia k déystviyu, vy dólzhny prinýt' áktsii i preodolévát' vse ródy trúdnóstey. 3120.title: A Leaf Block Out Eyes
english_paragraphs: Long ago, there was a scholar who was very poor and wanted to find a way to get rich. One day, he read in a book, “If you find the leaf a mantis uses to hide itself while catching a cicada, no one will be able to see you.” Delighted, he ran to a tree to look for the leaf. After searching for a while, he finally found it. But he accidentally dropped it, and it got mixed up with the other leaves on the ground. He could no longer tell which one it was. So he took all the leaves home and tested them one by one. Each time, he held a leaf over his eyes and asked his wife, “Can you see me?” She always said, “Yes!” Eventually, she grew tired of the question and said without thinking, “No!” He immediately took that leaf with him and grabbed someone else’s belongings right in front of them. He was caught on the spot.

3367.title: Nails
english_paragraphs: There was once a boy who often lost his temper with other people. One day, his father told him, “Every time you lose your temper, hammer a nail into the wall around the backyard.”

On the first day, the boy hammered in 37 nails. Later, he found that controlling his temper was easier than hammering in nails, so he gradually lost his temper less and less often. At last, one day, he was able to control his emotions.
His father then told him, “From now on, every time you manage not to lose your temper, pull out a nail.” After a long time, the boy finally pulled out all the nails.

His father said, “Son, you’ve done well. But look at the little holes in this wall. They will always be there. The wall can never be the way it was before. So always remember: don’t carelessly drive nails into other people’s hearts.”

There was once a boy who often lost his temper with other people. One day, his father told him, “Every time you lose your temper, hammer a nail into the wall around the backyard.”

On the first day, the boy hammered in 37 nails. Later, he found that controlling his temper was easier than hammering in nails, so he gradually lost his temper less and less often. At last, one day, he was able to control his emotions.

His father then told him, “From now on, every time you manage not to lose your temper, pull out a nail.” After a long time, the boy finally pulled out all the nails.

His father said, “Son, you’ve done well. But look at the little holes in this wall. They will always be there. The wall can never be the way it was before. So always remember: don’t carelessly drive nails into other people’s hearts.”
russian_paragraphs: Одна́жды был ма́льчик, который ча́сто терял свой нрав с друго́ми людьми. Одна́жды его ба́тюшка ска́зал ему: «С всегда́, когда́ ты теряешь свой нрав, нажи́ми гвоздь в стену́ вокру́г за́днего двора́».

В пе́рвый день ма́льчик наби́л 37 гвоздей. По́зже он обнаружил, что управля́ть своим нра́вом былó легче, чем наби́ть гвозди, поэтому он постепе́нно стал терять свой нрав реже. Наконе́ц, одна́жды он смо́г контролировать свои эмо́ции.
Тогда́ его ба́тька ска́зал ему: «Впредь, кажды́й раз, когда́ ты уда́ешься не терять свой нрав, вы́тяни гвоздь». По́сле до́лгого вре́мени ма́льчик наконе́ц вы́тянул все гвозди.

Его ба́тька ска́зал: «Сын, ты гото́в. Но посмо́три на ма́ленькие дыры в э́той стене. Они всегда́ будут тут. Стена никогда́ не сможет быть такой, какой она была́ ра́нее. Поэтому всегда́ помни: не безала́берно нажи́ми гвозди в чу́вства других людей.»

3147.title: The Weight of a Glass of Water
english_paragraphs: A teacher was giving a lesson, and the students were listening attentively. “How much do you think this glass of water weighs?” the teacher asked, picking it up. Some students said 200 grams; others said 300.

“That’s right, it weighs only 200 grams. But how long could you hold it?” the teacher continued. “For one minute? No problem. For an hour? Your arm might start to ache. But what about a whole day? Or a week? You might need an ambulance!” Everyone laughed.

The teacher went on: “This glass of water is actually quite light, but the longer you hold it, the heavier it feels. Stress is the same. No matter how much you’re carrying, if you hold on to it long enough, it can become too much to bear. So we should set down our burdens from time to time, then pick them up again. That way, we can keep going longer.”

3163.title: A Cup
english_paragraphs: A wealthy man asked a Zen master, “I’ve spent my whole life making money. How much should I earn before I stop?”
The Zen master placed a cup on the table and began pouring water into it from a kettle. Even after the water overflowed and covered the entire table, he kept pouring until the kettle was empty.
The Zen master asked, “Do you understand now?”
The wealthy man replied, “I don’t understand what this means.”

The Zen master said, “The kettleful of water is all the money you earn in your lifetime, and the cup holds as much as you’ll need to spend. Anything you earn beyond what you need will simply overflow—you won’t be able to keep it.”

russian_paragraphs: Обе́зпече́нный муж спро́сил хозя́ина дзэ́на: «Я потра́тил всю́ жизнь на зарабо́ток денег. Ско́лько я должен зараба́тывать, перед тем как останови́ться?»
Хозя́ин дзэ́на поста́вил ча́шку на стол и нача́л влива́ть воду́ в неё из ча́йника. Да́же после того, как вода́ перепо́лни́ла и закри́ла весь стол, он продолжа́л лить, пока́ ча́йник не опусте́л.

3049.title: Deceive Oneself
english_paragraphs: Once upon a time, a thief saw a beautiful, large bell and wanted to carry it home. But the bell was so big and heavy that he could only think of one way to take it: break it into pieces and carry them home separately.

The thief found a large hammer and struck the bell hard. It made a loud sound that gave him a fright. He threw his arms around the bell, trying to muffle the sound—but how could he? The thief grew anxious. Wasn’t the ringing telling everyone he was stealing the bell?

The more he listened, the more frightened he became. Without thinking, he covered his ears with his hands. “I can’t hear it anymore!” he said happily. He thought no one else could hear it either, so he plugged his ears with cloth and struck the bell again and again. Its loud ringing carried far and wide. When people heard it, they came running and caught the thief.

Once upon a time, a thief saw a beautiful, large bell and wanted to carry it home. But the bell was so big and heavy that he could only think of one way to take it: break it into pieces and carry them home separately.

When people heard it, they came running and caught the thief.
russian_paragraphs: Одна́жды вор уви́дел краси́вый большо́й ко́локол и зажа́л его́ нести́ до́ма. Но ко́локол был насто́лько большо́й и тяжёло́й, что он смо́г приду́мать только один спо́соб, как его взять: разби́ть его́ на кусо́чки и нести́ их до́ма отде́льно.

Вор нашёл большо́й мо́лот и сильно уда́рил ко́локол. Он издал гро́мкий звук, который испугал его́. Он обнял ко́локол, пыта́ясь заглуши́ть звук — но как он мог это сделать? Вор стал беспоко́йным. Разве зво́н не говори́л всем, что он кра́дёт ко́локол?

Чем больше он слу́шал, тем бо́льше он испуга́лся. Без мы́сли он закры́л свои́ у́ши рука́ми. “Я больше не слы́шу его́!” — сча́стливо ска́зал он. Он ду́мал, что никто́ другóй тоже не слы́шит, поэтому закле́ил у́ши тканью и удари́л по ко́локолу сно́ва и сно́ва. Его́ гро́мкий зво́н разнёсся по всему́ окрýжéнию. Когда люди́ услы́шали его́, они при́бегали и поймали вора.
reading_paragraphs: Odnázhdy vor uvíděl krásivý bol'shóy kólokol i zhazhál egó nestí́ domóy. No kólokol byl nastól'ko bol'shóy i tyazhóly, chto on smóg pridumát' tol'ko odín spósob, kak ego vzyát': razbí́t' egó na kusóchki i nestí́ ikh domóy otdél'no.

Vor našél bol'shóy môlot i sil'no udaríl kólokol. On izdal gromký zvúkd, kotorýy ispugál yegó. On obnyál kólokol, pytáyas' zaglušit' zvúk — no kak on mog etó sdélat'? Vor stal bespokóynym. Razve zvón ne govoríl všem, chto on krádet kólokol?

Chém bol'she on slúshal, tém bólshe on ispugálsya. Bez mýsli on zakrýl svoí úshi rukámi. “Ya bol'she ne slýshu egó!” — schastlivo skázal on. On dômáal, chto niktó drugóy tozhe ne slýshit, poetomu zakléil úshi tkányu i udaríl po kólokolu snóva i snóva. Egó gromký zvón razniósya po vsemu okrúzhéru. Kogdá lyudí uslýshali egó, oni príbegali i poymali vora.

3391.title: Smart Child
english_paragraphs: One day, Grandma Wang saw someone selling apples by the roadside. She asked the vendor, “How much are the apples?” “Two yuan each,” he said. “Take your pick.”

Grandma Wang carefully picked out some apples. Just then, a little boy ran over and said, “Grandma, these apples are big and red. You should buy a few more!” Grandma Wang smiled. “All right, I’ll take your advice and buy a few more.” The boy grabbed an apple and ran off. After choosing eight apples, Grandma Wang gave the vendor sixteen yuan. To her surprise, he said, “Sorry, you still owe me two yuan. Your grandson took an apple too.”
Grandma Wang said in surprise, “I don’t have a grandson… Oh, I see! So that boy isn’t your son!”

2917.title: Apply Mechanically
english_paragraphs: A waiter at a restaurant asked a customer a riddle: “My mother and father had a child who is neither my brother nor my sister. Who is it?” The customer couldn’t answer, so the waiter told him, “It’s me.”

When the customer got home, he posed the same riddle to a friend: “My parents had a child who is neither my brother nor my sister. Who is it?” “I don’t know,” his friend said. “Who?” The customer answered, “A waiter.”
When we aren’t sure we truly understand something, repeating it to others as though we do is one of the most foolish things we can do.
2917.english_full:
A waiter at a restaurant asked a customer a riddle: “My mother and father had a child who is neither my brother nor my sister. Who is it?” The customer couldn’t answer, so the waiter told him, “It’s me.”

When the customer got home, he posed the same riddle to a friend: “My parents had a child who is neither my brother nor my sister. Who is it?” “I don’t know,” his friend said. “Who?” The customer answered, “A waiter.”

When we aren’t sure we truly understand something, repeating it to others as though we do is one of the most foolish things we can do.
russian_paragraphs: Официа́нт в рестора́не спра́шивает зака́зчика загадку: «У ма́мы и ба́тюшки есть ребёнок, который ни мой брат, ни моя сестра. Кто это?» Зака́зчик не смог дать отве́та, и официа́нт ска́зал ему: «Это я.»

Когда зака́зчик при́ехал домой, он задал ту́ же загадку своему другу: «У моих опеку́нов есть дитя́, который ни мой брат, ни моя сестра. Кто это?» «Не знаю,» ска́зал друг. «Кто?» Зака́зчик отве́тил: «Официа́нт.»
Когда мы не уверены, что и́скренне понима́ем что́-то, повторя́ть это другим, как бу́дто понима́ем, — одна из самых дура́цких вещей, которые мы можем сде́лать.
reading_paragraphs: Ofitsíant v restoráne spráshivaet zakázchika zagádku: «U mámy i bátyushki yest́ rýebionok, kotorý ni moy brat, ni moya sestrá. Tó kto éto?» Zakázchik ne smóg dát́ otvétá, i ofitsíant skázal yemú: «Éto ya.»

Kogdá zakázchik priéhal domóy, on zadál tú zh́e zagádku svóyemu drugu: «U moikh opékunóv yest́ dityá, kotorý ni moy brat, ni moya sestrá. Tó kto éto?» «Ne znáyu,» skázal drug. «Kto?» Zakázchik otvét́il: «Ofitsíant.»
Kogdá my ne uveréný, chto ískrenne ponimáyem chtó-to, povtorírat́ éto drugím, kak búdto ponimáyem, — odna iz samykh durátskíkh veshchéy, kotórye my mózhem sdélat́.

2990.title: A Mouse Without Confidence
english_paragraphs: There was a little mouse in the forest who thought it looked unimpressive and had few abilities. It felt it was at the very bottom of the animal world. So it went to the mountain god and begged him again and again to turn it into a cat. The mountain god agreed. But just a few days after becoming a cat, the little mouse had a new problem: cats were afraid of dogs! It went back to the mountain god and asked to be turned into a dog. Then it discovered that dogs were afraid of wolves, so it hurried back and asked to become a wolf. After changing into many different animals, the little mouse finally became an elephant. Now all the animals were afraid of it, and it was delighted. But after a while, it discovered that what elephants feared most was mice. Suddenly, the animal it admired most was a mouse again, so it ran back to beg the mountain god once more...
There is no use envying others, because everyone has weaknesses. Only by believing in yourself can you find the courage to defeat your rivals.

3025.title: “万” Is Hard to Write
english_paragraphs: Once, a merchant hired a teacher to teach his son Chinese characters. On the first day, the teacher drew one stroke on a piece of paper and said, “This is the character ‘一’ (one).” The boy studied hard. On the second day, the teacher drew two strokes and said, “This is ‘二’ (two).” On the third day, he drew three strokes and said, “This is ‘三’ (three).” The boy decided writing was easy and that he had already learned how to do it, so he asked his father to dismiss the teacher. A few days later, the merchant asked his son to write “万” (ten thousand). The boy worked on it all day but still could not finish. “Who knew ‘万’ would be so hard to write?” he said. “I’ve been writing all day, and I’ve only managed 3,000 strokes.”
There is no end to what we can learn. If we are content with only a little understanding, how are we any different from this foolish son?

Once, a merchant hired a teacher to teach his son Chinese characters. On the first day, the teacher drew one stroke on a piece of paper and said, “This is the character ‘一’ (one).” The boy studied hard. A few days later, the merchant asked his son to write “万” (ten thousand). The boy worked on it all day but still could not finish. “Who knew ‘万’ would be so hard to write?” he said. “I’ve been writing all day, and I’ve only managed 3,000 strokes.”

russian_paragraphs: Оди́н раз купе́ц наня́л наста́вника, чтобы тот научи́л его́ сына кита́йским ие́роглифам. В пе́рвый день наста́вник нарисо́вал одну́ черту́ на бума́ге и ска́зал: «Э́то ие́роглиф „一“ (о́дин).» Ма́льчик у́сердно учи́лся. На втро́й день наста́вник нарисо́вал две черты́ и ска́зал: «Э́то „二“ (два).» На тре́тий день он нарисо́вал три черты́ и ска́зал: «Э́то „三“ (три).» Ма́льчик ре́шил, что пи́сать про́сто и что он уже́ нау́чился э́тому, поэтому он спроси́л отца, чтобы тот отпустил наста́вника. Че́рез не́сколько дней купе́ц спроси́л сына, чтобы тот написа́л „万“ (де́сять ты́сяч). Ма́льчик работал над э́тим ве́сь день, но всё е́ще не смог коне́чить. «Кто зна́л, что „万“ будет так жёстко́ к пи́санию?» ска́зал он. «Я пи́сал ве́сь день, и смо́г на́писать только 3000 черт.»
Нет конц́а тому, чему мы можем нау́читься. Если мы удово́льствова́ем лишь не́большим понима́нием, как мы отлича́емся от э́того глу́пого сына?

2941.title: Better Late Than Never
english_paragraphs: Once upon a time, a man kept many sheep. One morning, as he was getting ready to take them out to graze, he noticed that one was missing. It turned out there was a hole in the sheep pen. During the night, a wolf had crawled through it and carried off a sheep. His neighbor advised him, “Hurry and fix the pen. Block up that hole!” But the man said, “The sheep is already gone. What’s the point of fixing the pen now?” So he ignored his neighbor’s advice.

The next morning, as he was getting ready to take the sheep out to graze, he found that another one was missing. The wolf had crawled through the hole again and carried off another sheep. He regretted not listening to his neighbor, so he quickly blocked the hole and repaired the pen until it was strong and secure. From then on, no wolf ever carried off another of his sheep.
Even after you lose a sheep, fixing the pen can keep you from losing the rest. In the same way, correcting a mistake right away can prevent further mistakes and losses.
2941.english_full:
Once upon a time, a man kept many sheep. One morning, as he was getting ready to take them out to graze, he noticed that one was missing. It turned out there was a hole in the sheep pen. During the night, a wolf had crawled through it and carried off a sheep. His neighbor advised him, “Hurry and fix the pen. Block up that hole!” But the man said, “The sheep is already gone. What’s the point of fixing the pen now?” So he ignored his neighbor’s advice.

The next morning, as he was getting ready to take the sheep out to graze, he found that another one was missing. The wolf had crawled through the hole again and carried off another sheep. He regretted not listening to his neighbor, so he quickly blocked the hole and repaired the pen until it was strong and secure. From then on, no wolf ever carried off another of his sheep.

Even after you lose a sheep, fixing the pen can keep you from losing the rest. In the same way, correcting a mistake right away can prevent further mistakes and losses.
russian_paragraphs: Оди́н раз, дя́дя держал мно́гие овцы. О́дним у́тром, когда́ он гото́вился вы́вести их на пасу́шку, он заме́тил, что одна́ овца́ отсу́тствует. Оказа́лось, что в заго́не есть ка́рцер. Во вре́мя ночи́, волк про́полз через него и ута́щил овцу́. Его́ сосе́д посове́товал ему: «Спе́шите и по́чините заго́н. Заблоки́руйте этот ка́рцер!» Но дя́дя ска́зал: «Овца́ уже́ ушла. Како́й смысл по́чинить заго́н сейча́с?» Так он игнорирова́л сове́т сосе́да.

На следу́ющее у́тро, когда́ он гото́вился вы́вести овец на пасу́шку, он на́шёл, что ещё одна́ овца́ отсу́тствует. Волк про́полз через ка́рцер снова́ и ута́щил ещё одну овцу́. Он сожале́л, что не слуша́л своего́ сосе́да, поэтому он бы́стро заблоки́ровал ка́рцер и по́чинил заго́н, пока́ он не стал мо́щным и надёжным. С тех пор ни один волк никогда не ута́щил другую его овцу́.

Даже после того, как вы потеря́ли овцу́, по́чинка заго́на может предотврати́ть потерю остальных. Так же, как и исправле́ние оши́бки немедленно может предотврати́ть и́збежание дальне́йших оши́бок и поте́р.

3105.title: Value of Life
english_paragraphs: At a speech, a famous speaker held up a twenty-dollar bill and asked, “Who wants this twenty dollars?” Many hands went up. He continued, “I’m going to give it to one of you, but first, please let me do something.” He crumpled the bill into a ball and asked, “Who still wants it?” Some hands remained raised.

Then he said, “What if I do this?” He threw the bill on the ground and stepped on it. By now, it was dirty and wrinkled. “Who still wants it?” he asked. Some hands went up again. Finally, the speaker said, “My friends, no matter what I do to this bill, it is still worth twenty dollars. As we go through life, we may face many failures and even feel worthless. But remember: each of us has our own unique worth, and you will never lose yours!”

But remember: each of us has our own unique worth, and you will never lose yours!”
russian_paragraphs: На реч̧и изве́стный спи́кер поднёс ве́ксель на два́дцать долларов и спро́сил: «Кто хо́чет эти два́дцать долларов?» Мно́гие ру́ки поднима́лись. Он продолже́л: «Я собира́юсь дать это о́дному из вас, но сперва позво́льте мне сде́лать кое-что.» Он ско́мкал ве́ксель в ку́лачок и спро́сил: «Кто всё ещё хо́чет его?» Неско́лько ру́к оста́лись поднятыми.

Тогда́ он ска́зал: «А что, если я сде́лаю это?» Он бро́сил ве́ксель на земля́ и на́ступил на него. Теперь он был гри́зный и смя́тый. «Кто всё ещё хо́чет его?» – спроси́л он. Неско́лько ру́к поднима́лись опя́ть. Наконе́ц, спи́кер ска́зал: «Друзья́, неза́висимо от того, что я де́лаю с этим ве́кселем, он всё ещё сто́ит два́дцать долларов. Когда́ мы прохо́дим через жизнь, мы можем столкну́ться со многими неуда́чами и даже чува́ствовать себя ни́чем. Но помните: ка́ждый из нас име́ет свою уника́льную ценность, и вы никогда́ не потеря́ете свою!»

On prodolzhél: «Ya sobiráyus’ dát’ eto ódnomu iz vas, no sperva pozvólite mne sdélát’ kojé-čo.» On skomkal véksel v kúlačók i sprósil: «Kto vsyo yeshchó khóchét yego?» Néskol’ko rúk ostalís’ podnimátymi.

Togdá on skázal: «A čto, esli ya sdéláyú èto?» On brósil véksel na zemlyá i nästupíl na nevo. Tépera on byl grízný i smyátyj. «Kto vsyo yeshchó khóchét yego?» – sprósil on. 2847.title: Boxer’s Mistake
english_paragraphs: A tall boxer went to a restaurant for a meal. He took off his coat and hung it by the door. Worried that someone might take it, he left a note on it: “This coat belongs to a boxer. I’ll be back soon.” Then he went to eat, confident his coat was safe. But when he finished and went to get it, the coat was gone. All that remained was a note saying, “An outstanding runner took the coat. He won’t be coming back!”

Everyone has their own strengths. You may have strengths others lack, and others may have strengths you don’t. Don’t focus so much on what you’re good at that you overlook your weaknesses. It’s important to recognize other people’s strengths and your own shortcomings.

russian_paragraphs: Высо́кий боксёр пришёл в рестора́н поеда́ть. Он сня́л своё пальто́ и пови́сел его́ у две́ри. Беспоко́йный, что кто́-то может его́ взять, он остави́л на нём поме́тку: «Э́то пальто́ принадле́жит боксёру. Я ско́ро верну́сь.» Тогда́ он пошёл есть, уве́ренный, что его́ пальто́ в безопа́сности. Но когда́ он зака́нчил и пошёл за ним, пальто́ уже не бы́ло. Осталась лишь поме́тка, гово́рившая: «Выдаю́щийся бегу́н взял пальто́. Он не вернётся!»

Все име́ют свои́ сильные стороны. Вы можете иметь сильные стороны, которых нет у дру́гих, а у дру́гих могут быть сильные стороны, которых нет у вас. Не сосредоточива́йтесь так уж сильно на том, что у вас хорошо́ получа́ется, чтобы не упуска́ть свои́ сла́бости. Важно признава́ть сильные стороны ино́гих люде́й и свои́ недоста́тки.
reading_paragraphs: Vysoḱij boksýor prish́ël v restoŕan poedátʹ. On snýal svóe pal'tó i povísel egó u dvéri. Bespokójnyj, chto któ-to mozhet egó viźatʹ, on ostavíl na nёm pométku: «Éto pal'tó prinadlézhit boksýoru. Ya skóro vernу́sʹ.» Togd́a on posh́ёл yestʹ, uvérennyj, chto egó pal'tó v bezopaśnosti. No kogdá on zakánchil i posh́ёл za nim, pal'tó uźhe ne býlo. Ostálasʹ lishʹ pométka, govorívshaya: «Vydájushchijsya begún vzýal pal'tó. On ne vernёtsʹ!»

Vse iméyut svói silʹnye storony. Vy mozhete imétʹ silʹnye storony, kotorykh net u drúgikh, a u drúgikh mogut bytʹ silʹnye storony, kotorykh net u vas. 2871.title: Don’t Forget to Cheer for Yourself
english_paragraphs: In life, we often cheer for others. But have you ever thought of cheering for yourself?

There was a four-year-old girl who loved drawing. She had scribbled all over the walls at home, leaving them a mess. Her mother had no choice but to set aside a special place for her to draw, but the girl still often drew outside that area. Her mother said angrily, “Do as you’re told, or no matter how well you draw, your dad and I won’t praise you anymore!” The little girl looked completely unconcerned and said, “I can praise myself!”

Though the girl was young, what she said made a lot of sense. Each of us is the main character on the stage of our own life. In the real world, you may still be unknown, but if you keep a balanced outlook, cheer yourself on more often, and persevere, you will succeed one day.

In life, we often cheer for others. But have you ever thought of cheering for yourself?

There was a four-year-old girl who loved drawing. She had scribbled all over the walls at home, leaving them a mess. Though the girl was young, what she said made a lot of sense. Each of us is the main character on the stage of our own life. In the real world, you may still be unknown, but if you keep a balanced outlook, cheer yourself on more often, and persevere, you will succeed one day.
russian_paragraphs: В жи́зни мы ча́сто аплоди́руем други́м. Но вы когда́-либо ду́мали о том, чтобы поддержи́ть себя́?

Бы́ла де́вочка четырёх ле́т, кото́рая люби́ла рисова́ть. Она́ нацара́пала всевозмо́жные рисунки на стенах до́ма, оста́вив их в барда́ке. У её ма́тери не было вы́бора, кроме как отвести осо́бое место для рисова́ния, но де́вочка все́ равно ча́сто рисова́ла за гра́ницами этой площа́ди. Её ма́ть ска́зала гне́вно: «Де́лай, как тебе ска́жут, иначе, нева́жно, наско́лько хорошо́ ты рису́ешь, мы с твоим па́пой больше не будем тебя́ хвали́ть!» Де́вочка выгляде́ла вполне беззабо́тно и ска́зала: «Я сама́ могу себя́ хвали́ть!»

Хотя де́вочка была́ молода́, то, что она́ ска́зала, имело много смысла. Каждому из нас предстоя́т сво́й главны́й персона́ж на сцене́ своёй собстве́нной жи́зни. В реа́льном мире вы всё еще́ может быть неве́сты́, но если вы сохрани́те уравнове́женную точку зре́ния, чаще будете поддержи́вать себя́ и будете добива́ться своих це́лей, вы однажды обя́зательно преуспе́ете.

2817.title: Big Stone
english_paragraphs: Once upon a time, there was a large stone in front of a family’s house. It got in everyone’s way as they came and went, and people often tripped over it.

One day, the family’s son asked his father, “Dad, that stone in front of the house is dangerous. Let’s move it together!” His father smiled and replied, “That stone is very heavy. It was already there when my grandfather was alive. If it were that easy to move, do you think it would still be there now?”

But the son did not give up. The next day, he used a hoe to dig away the soil around the stone. To his surprise, the whole stone soon came loose. He quickly called some people to help, and they moved it with ease.

Sometimes, what stops us from discovering and creating new things is what we have always assumed to be true. If we have never really tried, how can we know for sure that things will turn out the way we expect?

2709.title: Dog’s Enemy
english_paragraphs: A dog stood in front of a mirror and spotted an enemy. It thought, “I’ve never seen this fellow before. I don’t know how tough it is, so I’ll watch it first.” But the dog noticed that the enemy was watching it too and didn’t seem the least bit afraid.

The dog grew a little nervous. It decided this fellow would be hard to deal with, so it tried to scare the enemy away. “Woof, woof! Woof, woof, woof!” it barked. The dog thought the enemy would run away, but to its surprise, the enemy in the mirror barked right back. “Looks like I’ve met my match today,” the dog thought. Then it opened its mouth wide and showed its sharp teeth. In its experience, all its enemies were afraid of its teeth. But this enemy wasn’t afraid at all—it showed even more frightening teeth.
The dog was terrified. In the end, it fled in a panic.

Я не зна́ю, на́сколько он жёсткий, поэ́тому я по́смотрю на него́ спа́рва.» Но соба́ка заме́тила, что во́раг смотри́т на неё́ та́кже и, похоже, совсем не бо́ится.

Соба́ка немно́го испу́гана. Она́ реши́ла, что э́тому рове́снику будет тру́дно рассма́тривать, поэ́тому она́ попы́талась испуга́ть во́рага. «Гав, гав! Гав, гав, гав!» — зала́яла она́. Соба́ка поду́мала, что во́раг убежа́т, но к её не́ожиданности во́раг в зе́ркале зала́ял в отве́т. «Похоже, я сегодн́я встре́тила свою́ противни́цу,» — поду́мала соба́ка. Затем она́ раскрыл́а рот ша́рико и вы́стала свои́ остро́й зубы. По её о́пыту, все́ её во́раги бо́я́лись её зубо́в. Но э́тому во́рагу во́все не было́ стра́шно — он́ вы́ставил ещё бо́лее пуга́ющие зубы.
Соба́ка была́ в ужасе. В коне́ц концо́в, она́ убе́гла в па́нике.

2734.title: Happiness
english_paragraphs: A group of young people searched everywhere for happiness, but instead they encountered many worries and hardships. They asked their teacher, Socrates, “Where exactly can we find happiness?” Socrates said, “Why don’t you help me build a boat first?”

The young people put their search for happiness aside for the time being. After 49 days, they had made a dugout canoe. They invited their teacher aboard, and as they paddled, they sang together. Socrates asked, “Are you happy, my children?” The students replied, “Very happy!”
Socrates said, “That’s how happiness works. It often comes to visit unexpectedly when you’re busy doing something else.”
2734.english_full:
A group of young people searched everywhere for happiness, but instead they encountered many worries and hardships. They asked their teacher, Socrates, “Where exactly can we find happiness?” Socrates said, “Why don’t you help me build a boat first?”

The young people put their search for happiness aside for the time being. After 49 days, they had made a dugout canoe. They invited their teacher aboard, and as they paddled, they sang together. Socrates asked, “Are you happy, my children?” The students replied, “Very happy!”

Socrates said, “That’s how happiness works. It often comes to visit unexpectedly when you’re busy doing something else.”
russian_paragraphs: Гру́ппа молодых лю́дей искала сча́стье всю́ду, но вместо этого они столкну́лись с мно́гими беспоко́йствами и тру́дностями. Они спра́шивали своего наста́вника, Сокра́та: «Где же то́чно мы можем на́йти сча́стье?» Сократ ска́зал: «Почему́ бы вам не помо́гать мне пострóить ло́дку пе́рвым делом?»

Молодые лю́ди отложи́ли свой по́иск сча́стья в сто́рону на теку́щий моме́нт. По́сле 49 дне́й они сде́лали долблёнку. Они пригласи́ли своего наста́вника на борт, и пока они гребли, они пели вме́сте. Сократ спра́шивал: «Вы счастли́вы, мои́ де́ти?» Студе́нты отве́тили: «Очень счастливы!»
Сократ ска́зал: «Вот как рабо́тает сча́стье. Оно ча́сто прихо́дит в неожи́данный визи́т, когда вы за́няты де́лом.»

Molodýe lyúdi otlózhili svói póisk schást'a v stóronu na tekúshchiy moment. Pósle 49 dney oni sdélali dolblyónku. Oni priglasíli svóego nastávnika na bórt, i poka oni grebli, oni peli vméste. Sokrat spráshival: «Vy schastlívy, moí déti?» Studénty otvetíli: «Óchen' schastlívy!»

2789.title: Giving Is Happiness
english_paragraphs: Once upon a time, there was a king who dearly loved his son. The young prince could have anything he wanted, yet he often wore a frown and was very unhappy.
One day, a man came to the palace and told the king that he knew how to make the prince happy. The king replied with delight, “If you can really do that, I’ll grant you anything you ask for.”

The man gave the prince a letter and told him to follow its instructions. The prince did as it said, and before long, he became the happiest young person in the kingdom. As it turned out, the letter contained just a few words: “Do one good deed for someone else every day!”
2789.english_full:
Once upon a time, there was a king who dearly loved his son. The young prince could have anything he wanted, yet he often wore a frown and was very unhappy.

One day, a man came to the palace and told the king that he knew how to make the prince happy. The king replied with delight, “If you can really do that, I’ll grant you anything you ask for.”

The man gave the prince a letter and told him to follow its instructions. The prince did as it said, and before long, he became the happiest young person in the kingdom. As it turned out, the letter contained just a few words: “Do one good deed for someone else every day!”
russian_paragraphs: Одна́жды, давным-давно, был король, который лю́бил своего́ сы́на. Молодо́й принц мог име́ть всё, что он жела́л, но он ча́сто насу́пливал брови́ и был очень несча́стным.

Одна́жды к дворе́цу пришёл муж и ска́зал коро́лю, что он зна́ет, как сделать принца сча́стливым. Король с радостью ответи́л: «Если вы деи́стви́тельно можете это сделать, я дам вам всё, что вы попроси́те.»

Муж дал принцу письмο и ска́зал ему следовать инстрýкциям. Принц сде́лал, как было сказа́но, и вскоре стал сча́стливейшим молоды́м челове́ком в короле́встве. Как вскоре вы́яснилось, письмо соде́ржало всего́ не́сколько слов: «Сде́лай одно́ до́брое де́ло для кого́-то друго́го ка́ждый день!»

Odnázhdy k dvorétsu prishël muzh i skázal korol'u, chto on znáet, kak sdelát' printśa schastlivym. Korol' s radúshchyu otvetíl: «Esli vy deýstvitel'no mozhete eto sdelát', ya dam vam vsyo, chto vy poprosíte.»

3033.title: Strength and Weakness
english_paragraphs: When two business owners met, they began sharing their experiences running their companies. One complained, “I can’t put up with three of my employees. One is always finding fault and complaining about everything. Another worries constantly about things that make no sense. And the third does no work and likes to wander around outside.” The other owner thought for a moment and said, “Why not let all three come work for me? That will save you the trouble of firing them.” The first owner happily agreed.

The next day, the three employees reported to their new company. Their new boss had already found a job for each of them: the one who always found fault was put in charge of quality control; the one who worried about everything was put in charge of safety and security; and the one who liked wandering around was sent out to promote the company and conduct research. Before long, all three were doing excellent work, and the company grew rapidly as a result.

Sometimes, strengths and weaknesses are not absolute. Used well, a weakness can become a strength. The key is to have the wisdom and insight of the second business owner and to try looking at the same problem from different angles.

russian_paragraphs: Когда́ два владе́леца би́знеса встре́тились, они на́чали дели́ться своим о́пытoм по управле́нию своими компа́ниями. О́дин из них жа́ловался: "Я не могу сноси́ть тро́их моих рабо́тников. О́дин всегда́ нахо́дит вину́ и ны́т по пово́ду всего́. Други́й постоя́нно беспоко́ится о не́чём, что́ не имеет смысла. А тре́тий не выполня́ет рабо́ту и лю́бит блужда́ть на у́лице." Други́й владе́лец поду́мал мно́гие минуту и ска́зал: "Почему́ бы не позво́лить всем трои́м прийти́ рабо́тать на меня? Это спаса́т тебя от затрудне́ний с их уво́льнением." Первый владе́лец сча́стливо согласился.

На сле́дующий день тро́е рабо́тников пришли́ на свою но́вую компа́нию. Их но́вый шеф уже́ нашёл де́ло для ка́ждого из них: о́дин, кто всегда́ находил вину́, был поставлен отве́тственным за контро́ль ка́чества; о́дин, кто беспоко́ился обо всём, был назначен отве́тственным за безопа́сность и надёжность; а о́дин, кто лю́бит блужда́ть, был отправлен на́ luar и дóлжен был продви́нуть компани́ю и прове́сти иссле́дования. Скоро все трое на́чали де́лать отли́чную рабо́ту, и компа́ния быстро́ ра́сширялась в результа́те.

Иногда́ си́лы и сла́бости не абсолютные. Если́ использова́ть сла́бость хорошо́, она мо́жет стать си́лой. Клю́чевое — име́ть му́дрость и инса́йт вто́рого владе́ца би́знеса и попы́таться посмо́треть на ту же пробле́му с друго́й стороны.

chunks.transliteration: Na sléduyushchiy den' tróe rabótnikov prishlí na svoyu nóvuyu kompániyu.

chunks.text: Их но́вый шеф уже́ нашёл де́ло для ка́ждого из них: о́дин, кто всегда́ находил вину́, был поставлен отве́тственным за контро́ль ка́чества; о́дин, кто беспоко́ился обо всём, был назначен отве́тственным за безопа́сность и надёжность; а о́дин, кто лю́бит блужда́ть, был отправлен на́ luar и дóлжен был продви́нуть компани́ю и прове́сти иссле́дования.
chunks.text_en: Their new boss had already found a job for each of them: the one who always found fault was put in charge of quality control; the one who worried about everything was put in charge of safety and security; and the one who liked wandering around was sent out to promote the company and conduct research.

chunks.transliteration: Ikh nóvyy shef uzhé nashyol délo dlya kázhdogo iz nikh: ódin, kto vsegdá nakhodil vinú, byl postavlen otvétstvennym za kontról' káchestva; ódin, kto bespokóilsya obo vsyom, byl naznachen otvétstvennym za bezopásnost' i nadyozhnost'; a ódin, kto lyúbit bluzhdát', byl otpravlen ná luar i dólzhen byl prodvínut' kompaníyu i provésti isslédovaniya.

chunks.text: Скоро все трое на́чали де́лать отли́чную рабо́ту, и компа́ния быстро́ ра́сширялась в результа́те.
chunks.text_en: Before long, all three were doing excellent work, and the company grew rapidly as a result.

chunks.text: Иногда́ си́лы и сла́бости не абсолютные.
chunks.text_en: Sometimes, strengths and weaknesses are not absolute.

2629.title: Lost Girl
english_paragraphs: A little girl was crying by the side of the road. A police officer came over and asked, “What’s wrong, little one?”
Through her tears, the little girl said, “I want to go home, but I don’t know the way.”
The officer asked, “What’s your daddy’s name?”
The little girl said, “Darling!”
The officer asked, “What’s your mommy’s name?”
The little girl said, “Baby!”

2589.title: Cup
english_paragraphs: There is a cup with water in it. If I asked you, “What is this?”

What would you say? If I poured out the water and asked you the same question, what would you say then? When a cup is full of water, people might say, “It’s water.” When it’s full of milk, they might say, “It’s milk.” Only when there’s nothing in the cup do people say, “Look, it’s a cup.”
We are much the same. When our hearts are filled with wealth, prejudice, and power, we are no longer ourselves. People often want to have many things, yet struggle to truly be themselves.
2589.english_full:
There is a cup with water in it. If I asked you, “What is this?”

What would you say? If I poured out the water and asked you the same question, what would you say then? When a cup is full of water, people might say, “It’s water.” When it’s full of milk, they might say, “It’s milk.” Only when there’s nothing in the cup do people say, “Look, it’s a cup.”

We are much the same. When our hearts are filled with wealth, prejudice, and power, we are no longer ourselves. People often want to have many things, yet struggle to truly be themselves.
russian_paragraphs: Есть ча́шка с во́дой внутри. Если я спрошу́ вас: “Что это?”

Что бы вы сло́вили? Если я извле́к во́ду и спрошу́ вас тот же вопро́с, что бы вы сло́вили тогда? Когда ча́шка по́лна во́дой, лю́ди можут сказать: “Это во́да.” Когда она по́лна молоком, они можут сказать: “Это молоко́.” Только когда в ча́шке ничто́, люди говорят: “Смотри́те, это ча́шка.”
Мы очень похо́жи. Когда наши че́рви запо́лнены бога́тством, предрассу́дками и вла́стью, мы уже́ не се́бя. Лю́ди часто хотят иметь много вещей, но борются, чтобы и́скренне быть се́бой.
reading_paragraphs: Yest' cháshka s vôdoy vnutri. Yesli ya spróshu vas: “Chto éto?”

Chto by vy slóvili? Yesli ya izvlék vôdu i spróshu vas tot zhe vapró s, chto by vy slóvili togda? Kogda cháshka pólna vôdoy, lýudi môzhut skazát': “Eto vôda.” Kogda ona pólna molokóm, oni môzhut skazát': “Eto molokó.” Tol'ko kogda v cháshke níchto, lýudi govorât: “Smotrite, eto cháshka.”
My óchen' pókhzhi. Kogda náshe chérvi zapólneny bagátsvom, predrassúdkami i vlástý, my uzhé ne sébya. Lýudi chástо khotyát imét' mnogo véshchey, no bôrrýutsya, chtoby ískrenne byt' séboy.

2541.title: Please Don’t Open the Wrong Window
2541.russian_title: Пожа́луйста, не откры́вайте не то око́но
english_paragraphs: A little girl stood by the window, watching people outside bury their beloved puppy. The sight made her so sad that she began to cry.

Her grandfather saw her and quickly led her to another window, where she could look out at a beautiful garden. The flowers were lovely, and sure enough, the little girl felt better as soon as she saw them. Before long, she was smiling happily. Her grandfather said, "You were looking out the wrong window, my child. See? When you look out a different window, doesn't the world seem different?"
When you face failure, don't be too sad. Open the window beside it, and perhaps you'll find hope.
2541.english_full:
A little girl stood by the window, watching people outside bury their beloved puppy. The sight made her so sad that she began to cry.

Her grandfather saw her and quickly led her to another window, where she could look out at a beautiful garden. The flowers were lovely, and sure enough, the little girl felt better as soon as she saw them. Before long, she was smiling happily. Her grandfather said, "You were looking out the wrong window, my child. See? When you look out a different window, doesn't the world seem different?"

When you face failure, don't be too sad. Open the window beside it, and perhaps you'll find hope.
russian_paragraphs: Де́вочка стаяла у окна́ и смотри́ла, как лю́ди за́бывают своего люби́мого ку́тёнка. Вид мог за́грустить её, и она́ нача́ла плака́ть.

Её де́душка у́видел её и бы́стро привёл её к друго́му око́ну, откуда она́ могла́ смотри́ть на краси́вый сад. Цветы́ бы́ли восхити́тельными, и, как ни́ в чём не бы́ло, де́вочка на́конец чувстовала́ себя́ лу́чше, как то́лько она́ их уви́дела. 2685.title: Imagination Is More Important
english_paragraphs: If you had to fight someone, would you choose an ordinary person or a karate champion? Most people would probably choose the ordinary person, because everyone knows a karate champion is good at fighting.

But there is a story from the United States: two people got into a fight over something trivial. One was an ordinary person, and the other was a famous karate champion. A few minutes later, the result was clear—the karate champion had lost. The champion was constrained by the rules and would not strike the other person's head. But the ordinary person had never learned those rules. He punched the champion hard in the nose, and the champion could not get back up.
So imagination is more important than knowledge!
2685.english_full:
If you had to fight someone, would you choose an ordinary person or a karate champion? Most people would probably choose the ordinary person, because everyone knows a karate champion is good at fighting.

But there is a story from the United States: two people got into a fight over something trivial. One was an ordinary person, and the other was a famous karate champion. A few minutes later, the result was clear—the karate champion had lost. The champion was constrained by the rules and would not strike the other person's head. But the ordinary person had never learned those rules. He punched the champion hard in the nose, and the champion could not get back up.

So imagination is more important than knowledge!
russian_paragraphs: Если вы́ должны́ дра́ться с кем-то, вы́ вы́берете обыкнове́нного челове́ка или чемпио́на по карате́? Вероя́тно, бу́дут большинст́во людéй вы́бирать обыкнове́нного челове́ка, потому что все зна́ют, что чемпио́н по карате́ хоро́ший бо́рющийся.

Но есть исто́рия из Соединённых Шта́тов: двое людей попа́ли в дра́ку из-за чего́-то незначи́тельного. Один был обыкнове́нным челове́ком, а друго́й — знамени́тым чемпио́ном по карате́. Нескóлько мину́т по́сле результат был я́сен — чемпио́н по карате́ потеря́л. Чемпио́н был принужда́ем правилами и не мог уда́рить голову друго́го челове́ка. Но обыкнове́нный челове́к никогда́ не у́чил эти правила. Он уда́рил чемпио́на кре́пко в нос, и чемпио́н не смог верну́ться назад.
Поэ́тому воображе́ние более ва́жно, чем зна́ние!
reading_paragraphs: Eslí vý dolzhný drátsya s kem-to, vý výberete obýknovenngo chelovéka ili chempióna po karaté? Veroyátno, búdyt bol'shinst́vo lyúdей výbirat' obýknovenngogo chelovéka, potomu chto vse znáyut, chto chempión po karaté khóroshii borjúshchii.

No yest' istóriya iz Soyedinyónnykh Shtátov: dvoye lyudey popáli v dráku iz-za chegó-to neznáchitel'nogo. Odin byl obýknovenym chelovékom, a drugóy — známenitym chempiónom po karaté. Neskól'ko minút poźle rezul'tat byl yásen — chempión po karaté poteryál. Chempión byl prinuzhdáem pravílami i ne mog udarít' golovu drugógo chelovéka. No obýknovennyi chelovék nikogdá ne uchíl eti pravila. On udaríl chempióna krépko v nos, i chempión ne smóg vernút'sya nazad.
Poétemu voobrazhéniye bolée vázhno, chem znániye!

2433.title: I`m thirsty
english_paragraphs: Mom: What’s wrong?
Child: Mom, I’m tired… and I’m really thirsty, too.
Mom: Sit here. How do you feel now?
Child: A little better.
Mom: Look! There’s some cola over there! I’ll go buy some.
Mom: Here, have a drink!
Child: Thanks, Mom. It tastes great.
Mom: Do you feel better now?
Child: Yes, I feel better now. Thanks, Mom!

2764.title: Spend 90% of the Time Considering Failure
english_paragraphs: Li Ka-shing is a famous Chinese business magnate. A reporter once asked him, “People are curious: over more than half a century, how have you managed to expand your business around the world while avoiding major setbacks?”

Li replied, “I often spend 90% of my time thinking about failure.” He went on to explain, “I constantly examine the problems that might arise in each project. It’s like a ship preparing to leave port: it must plan how to cope if it encounters a typhoon.”
The reporter asked, “Most people are focused on how to succeed. Why do you spend 90% of your time thinking about failure?”

Li answered calmly, “You must think about failure first. If even one part of a company develops a problem, the whole company could collapse... The more thoroughly you consider every possible failure, the greater your chances of success.”

russian_paragraphs: Ли Ка-ши́н — изве́стный кита́йский магнат би́знеса. Одна́жды репорте́р спра́шивал у него: «Лю́ди любопы́тны: за по́чти полове́ну века, как вам удалос́ь расширить свой би́знес во всех ча́стях ми́ра, избегая серьёзных препя́тствий?»

Ли отве́тил: «Я ча́сто тра́чу 90% своего вре́мени на мышле́ние о прова́ле.» Он продолжа́л объясня́ть: «Я постоя́нно осма́трю про́блемы, которые могут возни́кнуть в ка́ждом прое́кте. Это похо́жий на су́дно, гото́вящееся к отплы́тию из порта: оно должно́ плани́ровать, как справи́ться, если его застанет тайфу́н.»
Репорте́р спра́шивал: «Наи́большее количество люде́й сосредоточься на том, как преуспе́ть. Почему́ вы тра́тите 90% своего вре́мени на мышле́ние о прова́ле?»

Ли споко́йно отве́тил: «Вы должны́ в пер́вую о́чередь обду́мывать прова́л. Если да́же одна́ часть компа́нии разовьёт про́блему, вся́ компа́ния может колла́псировать... Чем осно́вательнее вы рассматри́ваете ка́ждый возмо́жный прова́л, тем бо́льше шансов на уда́чу.»

2637.title: Two Hours of Life Changing
english_paragraphs: At a class reunion, one former classmate caught everyone’s attention because he had become very successful in his career. But as they remembered him, he had never been an outstanding student. His grades and abilities had been fairly average.
Later, someone asked him, “What’s the secret to your success?” He replied, “There’s really no secret. I just spent most of my time on one thing.”

It turned out that after graduating from college, he had set aside two hours every day to study business management. A few years later, he started his own company. With all the knowledge he had gained, his company quickly grew larger and larger.
2637.english_full:
At a class reunion, one former classmate caught everyone’s attention because he had become very successful in his career. But as they remembered him, he had never been an outstanding student. His grades and abilities had been fairly average.

Later, someone asked him, “What’s the secret to your success?” He replied, “There’s really no secret. I just spent most of my time on one thing.”

It turned out that after graduating from college, he had set aside two hours every day to study business management. A few years later, he started his own company. With all the knowledge he had gained, his company quickly grew larger and larger.
russian_paragraphs: На воссоедине́нии класса о́дин бы́вший однокла́ссник привлёк все́х своим успехом в карье́ре. Но, вспоми́ная о нём, все́ поня́ли, что он никогда́ не был выдаю́щимся студе́нтом. Его́ оценки и спосо́бности бы́ли сре́дними.
По́зже кто́-то спра́шивает у него: «Како́й секрет тво́его успеха?» Он отвечает: «На самом деле, секрета нет. Я прост́о проводи́л больша́я часть своего́ вре́мени за однóй вещью.»

2677.title: Smart Hawker
english_paragraphs: A man went to buy some milk. The vendor said, “Three yuan a cup, or ten yuan for three cups.”
The man paid three yuan for a cup and did the same thing two more times. Then he said to the vendor, “See? I got three cups for just nine yuan.”
The vendor said, “When I price it this way, I sell three cups every time.”

The man paid three yuan for a cup and did the same thing two more times. Then he said to the vendor, “See? I got three cups for just nine yuan.”

The vendor said, “When I price it this way, I sell three cups every time.”

2508.title: Fishing
english_paragraphs: An old man was fishing when a child came over to watch him. The old man thought the child was adorable and offered to give him all the fish he had caught. But the child shook his head. Puzzled, the old man asked, “Why don’t you want them?”
The child replied, “Grandpa, I love eating fish, but these fish will soon be gone. If you teach me how to fish, I can catch my own, and I’ll have fish to eat for the rest of my life.”

An old man was fishing when a child came over to watch him. The old man thought the child was adorable and offered to give him all the fish he had caught. But the child shook his head. Puzzled, the old man asked, “Why don’t you want them?”

The child replied, “Grandpa, I love eating fish, but these fish will soon be gone. If you teach me how to fish, I can catch my own, and I’ll have fish to eat for the rest of my life.”

Ребёнок ответи́л: «Деду́ля, я любо́вь к еде́ люблю́, но эти ры́бы вскоре исче́знут. Если ты научи́шь меня, как рыба́чить, я смогу́ пойма́ть свою́ и у меня бу́дут ры́бы, чтобы ку́шать оставшуюся жи́знь.»

2361.title: Make the Loss Cute
english_paragraphs: A man bought a new pair of shoes that he liked very much, so he wore them on the train to visit his girlfriend. But during the ride, one of his shoes fell off the train. Everyone thought it was a shame, but he immediately threw the other shoe off too. Everyone was puzzled. The man said, “One shoe is no use to me now, but if someone finds the pair, they might be able to wear them!”

2441.title: Gold Egg
english_paragraphs: One morning, a farmer discovered that his hen had laid a golden egg. Delighted, he took the egg home. From then on, he found a golden egg every morning, and he grew richer and richer. But the farmer also grew greedier and greedier. He thought one golden egg a day was too slow, so he killed the hen to get all the golden eggs he imagined were inside her. But there was nothing inside, and he became poor again.

2392.title: Two Daughters
english_paragraphs: An elderly woman had two daughters. Her older daughter sold straw sun hats, and her younger daughter sold umbrellas. The woman looked worried every day.

A neighbor asked her why. The woman said, “When it rains, I worry that my older daughter won’t be able to sell her sun hats. But when the sun comes out, I worry that my younger daughter won’t be able to sell her umbrellas. How could I not worry?”

The neighbor smiled and said, “Whenever it rains, your younger daughter’s umbrellas sell especially well. And when the sun comes out, more customers visit your older daughter’s shop. Whether it’s sunny or rainy, things work out well for them. How enviable!”
The way you look at things determines your quality of life. What matters most is having a positive, optimistic attitude.

russian_paragraphs: Ста́рая же́нщина имела две до́чки. Её старша́я до́чка продавала соло́менные ша́пки, а её младше́й до́чке прода́ли зо́нтики. Женщина смотрела беспоко́йно ка́ждый день.

О́бщая сусе́дка спроси́ла её, почему́. Женщина ска́зала: «Когда́ идёт дождь, я беспокоюсь, что моя старша́я до́чка не смо́жет продать свои ша́пки. Но когда́ со́лнце вы́ходит, я беспокоюсь, что моя младше́й до́чке не уда́стся продать свои зо́нтики. Как я могу́ не волноваться?»

Сусе́дка улы́бнулась и ска́зала: «Когда́ идёт дождь, зо́нтики твоей младше́й до́чки продаются осо́бенно хоро́шо. А когда́ со́лнце вы́ходит, бо́льше клие́нтов посещают магази́н твоей старша́й до́чки. Нева́жно, со́лнечно ли или дождли́во, всё преуспева́ет для них. Как зави́дно!»
То, как ты смотри́шь на вещи, определи́вает твоё ка́чество жи́зни. Что имеет наибольшее значение – это име́ть положи́тельный, оптимисти́ческий настрой.

Óbshaya susédka sprosíla yeyo, pochemú. Zhénshchina skázala: «Kogdá idyót dózhd', ya bespokóyus', chto moya starsháya dóchka ne smózhét prodat' svoyi shápki. No kogdá sólnce vykhódit, ya bespokóyus', chto moya mládshya dóchka ne udátsya prodat' svoyi zónitiki. Kak ya mogú ne volnovat'sya?»

Susédka ulýbnulas' i skázala: «Kogdá idyót dózhd', zónitiki tvoyey mládshyay dóchki prodaiut'sya osóbenny khorosho. A kogdá sólnce vykhódit, ból'she kliéntov poseshchayut magazín tvoyey starsháy dóchki. Nevázhno, sólnéchno li ili dózhd'ivó, vsyo preuspeváĭet dlya nikh. Kak zavídno!»

2313.title: Puppy and kitten
english_paragraphs: The first time my puppy saw my friend's kitten, it was very scared.
The second time the puppy saw the kitten, it stood beside the kitten and watched it.
The third time it saw the kitten, it went over and played with it.
Soon, they became good friends.

The first time my puppy saw my friend's kitten, it was very scared.

The second time the puppy saw the kitten, it stood beside the kitten and watched it.

The third time it saw the kitten, it went over and played with it.

Soon, they became good friends.

2661.title: Swift Horse
english_paragraphs: There were two horses, one white and one black. The white horse was a swift horse, born strong and sturdy. The black horse was not quite as strong.

Because their owner’s income was unpredictable, the food he gave them was sometimes good and sometimes poor. The white horse adjusted its speed according to the food: when it ate well, it ran faster; when it didn’t, it ran slower. But no matter what food the owner gave them, the black horse always ran as hard as it could.

Gradually, the owner noticed that the white horse sometimes ran fast and sometimes ran slowly, while the black horse kept getting faster. So he always gave the black horse a little more food. This made the white horse even angrier. It thought, “If that’s how you treat me, I won’t run hard for you!”

After some time, the owner felt that the white horse could no longer run as fast as the black horse and was getting slower and slower. Finally, one day, he decided to send the white horse to work at the mill, turning the millstone.
2661.english_full:
There were two horses, one white and one black. The white horse was a swift horse, born strong and sturdy. The black horse was not quite as strong.

Because their owner’s income was unpredictable, the food he gave them was sometimes good and sometimes poor. The white horse adjusted its speed according to the food: when it ate well, it ran faster; when it didn’t, it ran slower. But no matter what food the owner gave them, the black horse always ran as hard as it could.

Gradually, the owner noticed that the white horse sometimes ran fast and sometimes ran slowly, while the black horse kept getting faster. So he always gave the black horse a little more food. This made the white horse even angrier. It thought, “If that’s how you treat me, I won’t run hard for you!”

After some time, the owner felt that the white horse could no longer run as fast as the black horse and was getting slower and slower. Finally, one day, he decided to send the white horse to work at the mill, turning the millstone.
russian_paragraphs: Там бы́ло две ло́шади, о́дна бе́лая и о́дна вороно́я. Бе́лая лошадь была бы́строй, урождённой сильной и дю́жей. Вороно́й ко́нь не был совсе́м таким же си́льным.

Потому что доход владе́льца был непредсказу́емым, еда, которую он да́л им, иногда́ была хо́рошей, а иногда́ жа́лкой. Бе́лая лошадь настра́ивала свою ско́рость в соотве́тствии с еду́: когда она ела хоро́шо, она бегала быстрее; когда нет, она бегала медленно. Но вне за́висимости от того, какую еду владе́лец да́л им, вороно́й ко́нь всегда́ бегал на́сколько мо́жно усерднее.

Постепе́нно владе́лец замеча́л, что бе́лая лошадь иногда́ бегала быстро, а иногда́ медленно, в то же вре́мя как вороно́й ко́нь стал бегать ещё быстрее. Поэтому он всегда́ да́вал вороно́му ко́ню немно́го бо́льше еды. Это сделало бе́лую лошадь даже ещё более разо́жжённой. Она думала: «Если ты так меня угоща́ешь, я не буду бегать усердно для тебя!»

По́сле како́го-то вре́мени владе́лец почу́ствовал, что бе́лая лошадь больше не могла бегать так быстро, как вороно́й ко́нь, и становилась всё более ме́дленной. Наконе́ц, одна́жды, он реши́л посыла́ть бе́лую лошадь на рабо́ту в ме́льницу, повора́чивая жёрнов.
reading_paragraphs: Tam býlo dve lóshadi, ódna bélaya i ódna voronóya. Bélaya lóshad' byla býstroi, urazhdyónnoi sil'noi i dyúzhei. Voronói kón' ne byl sovsém takim zhe sílnym.

Potomu chto dokhod vladél'tsa byl nepredskazúemym, eda, kotoruyu on dál im, inogdá byla khóroshoi, a inogdá zhal'koi. Bélaya lóshad' nastróivala svoyu skórost' v sootvetstvíi s edú: kogdá ona ela khórosho, ona begala bystree; kogda net, ona begala medlenno. No vne zavisimosti ot togo, kakúyu edu vladélets dál im, voronói kón' vsegdá begal náskol'ko mózhno userdnee.

Postepénno vladélets zamechá́l, chto bélaya lóshad' inogdá begala bystro, a inogdá medlenno, v to zhe vremya kak voronói kón' stal begat' eshchó bystree. Poetomu on vsegdá dával voronómu kónyu nemnógo bólshe edu. Éto sdelalo béluю lóshad' dazhe eshchó yeshche bolée razózhzhennoy. Ona dumala: «Esli ty tak menya ugościáesh', ya ne budu begat' userdno dlya tebya!»

Pósle kakógo-to vremeni vladélets pochústvoval, chto bélaya lóshad' bol'she ne mógla begat' tak bystro, kak voronói kón', i stanovilas' vsyo bolée medlennoy. Nakonét, odnázhdy, on reshíl posilát' béluю lóshad' na rabotu v mélnitsu, povoráchívaya zhérnov.

Бе́лаяBélaya лошадьloshad' былаbyla бы́стройbýstroy, урождённойurozhdyonnoy сильнойsil'noy иi дю́жейdyúzhey. Вороно́йVoronóy ко́ньkón' неne былbyl совсе́мsovsém такимtakim жеzhe си́льнымsíl'nym.

ПотомуPotomu чтоchto доходdokhod владе́льцаvladél'tsa былbyl непредсказу́емымnepredskazúemym, едаeda, которуюkotoruyu онon да́лdál имim, иногда́inogdá былаbyla хо́рошейkhóroshey, аa иногда́inogdá жа́лкойzhálkoy.
